# Comparing with AArch64 {#appendix-p-comparing-with-aarch64}

This appendix was added in this edition. x86-64 is not the only
processor family you will meet. Phones, tablets, the Raspberry Pi,
Apple\'s computers since 2020 and many servers in the cloud use the
64-bit ARM architecture, *AArch64* (also called *ARM64*). Linux works
the same on it: the same system calls, files, ELF programs and tools.
Seeing our first two programs written for it shows which parts of this
book are about x86-64 and which parts are about every computer.

Running AArch64 Programs on x86-64 {#running-aarch64-programs-on-x86-64}
----------------------------------

You don\'t need an ARM computer. On Ubuntu, the package
`binutils-aarch64-linux-gnu` has `as`, `ld` and `objdump` for AArch64,
with the prefix `aarch64-linux-gnu-`, and `qemu-user` has
`qemu-aarch64`, which runs an AArch64 Linux program on x86-64 by
translating its instructions:

```{.bash}
sudo apt install binutils-aarch64-linux-gnu qemu-user
aarch64-linux-gnu-as -g -o 0AP-01-exit-aarch64.o 0AP-01-exit-aarch64.s
aarch64-linux-gnu-ld -o 0AP-01-exit-aarch64 0AP-01-exit-aarch64.o
qemu-aarch64 ./0AP-01-exit-aarch64
echo $?
```

The First Program {#the-first-program-aarch64}
-----------------

This is `003-01-exit` for AArch64:

```{.gnuassembler .numberLines include=resource/asm/0AP-01-exit-aarch64.s}
```

It is the same program with different names:

-   Comments start with `//` (in AArch64 assembly, `#` marks a number).

-   Registers have no `%`. The 64-bit registers are _x0_ to _x30_.

-   The operands are in the other order: the destination comes *first*,
    as in the Intel syntax of
    [Appendix B](appendix-b-common-x86-instructions.qmd#differences-in-other-syntaxes-and-terminology).
    `mov x8, #93` puts 93 in _x8_.

-   The system call number goes in _x8_, the parameters in _x0_ to _x5_,
    the result comes back in _x0_, and `svc #0` (*supervisor call*)
    plays the part of `syscall`. The numbers are different too: `exit`
    is 93 on AArch64 and 60 on x86-64. Linux has one table of numbers
    per architecture.

Finding a Maximum Value {#finding-a-maximum-value-aarch64}
-----------------------

This is `003-02-maximum` for AArch64. It returns 222, like the x86-64
version:

```{.gnuassembler .numberLines include=resource/asm/0AP-02-maximum-aarch64.s}
```

`aarch64-linux-gnu-objdump -d 0AP-02-maximum-aarch64` shows the
instructions with their machine code:

```{.text check=appp-objdump-maximum}
00000000004000e8 <_start>:
  4000e8:       90000081        adrp    x1, 410000 <done+0xfef0>
  4000ec:       91046021        add     x1, x1, #0x118
  4000f0:       d2800002        mov     x2, #0x0                        // #0
  4000f4:       f9400020        ldr     x0, [x1]

00000000004000f8 <loop>:
  4000f8:       f8627823        ldr     x3, [x1, x2, lsl #3]
  4000fc:       b40000a3        cbz     x3, 400110 <done>
  400100:       eb00007f        cmp     x3, x0
  400104:       9a80c060        csel    x0, x3, x0, gt
  400108:       91000442        add     x2, x2, #0x1
  40010c:       17fffffb        b       4000f8 <loop>

0000000000400110 <done>:
  400110:       d2800ba8        mov     x8, #0x5d                       // #93
  400114:       d4000001        svc     #0x0
```

The differences that matter:

-   **Every instruction is 4 bytes long.** The addresses go up by 4,
    and the decoder always knows where the next instruction starts,
    which is simpler and faster than decoding x86-64 (see
    [Decoding an Instruction](appendix-n-the-fetch-execute-cycle.qmd#decoding-an-instruction)).
    The price is that a 64-bit address or number doesn\'t fit in one
    instruction.

-   **That is why the address takes two instructions.** `adrp` puts in
    _x1_ the address of the 4096-byte page that holds `data_items`,
    computed relative to the instruction itself, like `%rip`-relative
    addressing (`410000` here). `add` adds the position of `data_items`
    inside that page (`:lo12:` means its lowest 12 bits, `0x118`). The
    program is still position-independent.

-   **Only loads and stores touch memory.** `ldr` (*load register*) and
    `str` (*store*) move data between memory and registers; `cmp`,
    `add` and every other operation work only on registers. On x86-64,
    `cmpq $0, (%rax)` reads memory and compares in one instruction.
    Architectures built this way are called *load/store* architectures.

-   **The addressing modes are similar.** `[x1, x2, lsl #3]` is
    _x1_ + _x2_ × 8, the same as `(%rbx,%rcx,8)`: `lsl #3` (*logical
    shift left* by 3) multiplies by 8.

-   **Some instructions do more.** `cbz` (*compare and branch if zero*)
    tests a register and jumps without touching the flags. `csel`
    (*conditional select*) is AArch64\'s `cmov`: it puts _x3_ in _x0_ if
    the last comparison said *greater* (`gt`), and _x0_ otherwise.

-   **The flags are set only when you ask.** AArch64 has four flags, N
    (negative), Z (zero), C (carry) and V (overflow), like SF, ZF, CF and
    OF. `cmp` sets them, but `add` doesn\'t; `adds` does. On x86-64
    almost every arithmetic instruction changes them.

Registers and the Calling Convention {#registers-and-the-calling-convention-aarch64}
------------------------------------

| | x86-64 | AArch64 |
|-|--------|---------|
| Registers for numbers | 16: _%rax_ ... _%r15_ | 31: _x0_ ... _x30_ |
| 32-bit halves | _%eax_ ...; writing one clears the upper half | _w0_ ... _w30_; writing one clears the upper half |
| Zero register | None | _xzr_ (reads as 0, writes are ignored) |
| Stack pointer | _%rsp_ | _sp_ |
| Parameters | _%rdi_, _%rsi_, _%rdx_, _%rcx_, _%r8_, _%r9_ | _x0_ to _x7_ |
| Return value | _%rax_ | _x0_ |
| Callee-saved | _%rbx_, _%rbp_, _%r12_ to _%r15_ | _x19_ to _x28_, _x29_ |
| Frame pointer | _%rbp_ | _x29_ |
| Return address | Pushed on the stack by `call` | Put in _x30_ (the *link register*) by `bl` |
| Stack alignment | 16 bytes at every `call` | 16 bytes whenever _sp_ is used to reach memory |
| Byte order | Little-endian | Little-endian (on Linux) |

The biggest difference is the return address. `bl function` (*branch
with link*) jumps to the function and puts the return address in _x30_,
not on the stack, and `ret` jumps to the address in _x30_. A function
that calls nothing never touches the stack. A function that calls
another one must save _x30_ first, usually together with the frame
pointer, in the two instructions that start most AArch64 functions:

```{.gnuassembler}
stp  x29, x30, [sp, #-16]!  // Store the pair at sp - 16,
                            // and move sp there.
mov  x29, sp                // The new frame pointer.
```

which do what `pushq %rbp` and `movq %rsp, %rbp` do, and save the
return address too. The function ends with `ldp x29, x30, [sp], #16`
and `ret`.

What Stays the Same {#what-stays-the-same-aarch64}
-------------------

Almost everything else in this book: memory as numbered bytes,
registers, the stack, functions and their parameters, system calls,
file descriptors and buffers, ELF files, sections and symbols, shared
libraries and position-independent code, `brk` and `mmap`, ASLR,
two\'s complement, IEEE 754 floating point, gdb, `strace` and `objdump`.
An assembly language is a set of names for one processor\'s
instructions; the ideas behind it are the same on every computer. For
the details of AArch64, see the
[Arm Architecture Reference Manual for A-profile][AP-ARM-ARM] and the
[Procedure Call Standard for the Arm 64-bit Architecture][AP-AAPCS64].

[AP-ARM-ARM]: https://developer.arm.com/documentation/ddi0487/latest
[AP-AAPCS64]: https://github.com/ARM-software/abi-aa/blob/main/aapcs64/aapcs64.rst
